headline: East End on the 6:04 Ebb: Bass Hold the Rip, Blues Crash the Seam
subhead: The moon's building toward full, current's coming back with authority, and the west end is one warm push from its first bonito of the year.
body_markdown:
Six-oh-four this morning. That's when the ebb hit max push off the Railroad Bridge, and I had a rod bent inside of ninety seconds. Thirty years I've watched that clock, and it still gets me every time — the current builds, the bait gets pinned against the seam, and for about ninety minutes on either side of max flow, the east end turns into the best piece of moving water on the Cape. Right now, in the thick of late July, that window is everything. Miss it and you're fishing dead water. Hit it and you're in business.

We flagged this pattern last week and said it'd hold as long as the warm, stable weather stuck around — and here we are. The Canal is running its classic mid-summer script: stripers stacked on the current seams, feeding hard on the strong tide stages, and going quiet in between. The difference this week is the moon. We're building toward full in early August, which means the tidal push through the ditch is getting stronger every day. Bigger swings mean harder current, and harder current means the rips are setting up sharper and the bite windows are getting more violent, if shorter.

East end first. The rip line off the Railroad Bridge and down toward Scusset has been the most consistent piece of structure all week, but only on the meat of the tide. Dawn ebb has been my money window — that 5:30 to 7:00 stretch when the sun's just up and the current's ripping hard enough to hold bait against the rocks. Bass to 34 inches have come on swimming plugs — a Redfin or a Danny-style glide, fished with the current, not against it, letting the plug swim naturally through the seam rather than burning it back. After dark it's a different game entirely. Water temp's sitting where it sits every late July — warm enough that the bass have gone mostly nocturnal, same as everywhere south of here. Daytime fish are holding deep in the thermocline seams and only really committing after the sun's down, so if you want quality, you fish the dark side of the strong tides. Eels on the drift, bunker chunks anchored up tight to the rock pile below Scusset — that's where the bigger fish are coming from, 15 to 25 pounds, mostly after 9 PM on the building ebb.

Bluefish are mixed right into those same lanes, and honestly some nights they've been thicker than the bass. Choppers to 8 pounds are hitting the same plugs, same current seams, same tide stages — no real separation between the two species right now, which means if you're targeting one you're going to catch the other. Keep a pair of pliers handy and expect some leader damage if you're running mono.

West end tells a slightly different story. Mashnee Island and the flats around Hog Island have been holding fluke — not a blitz, but a real fishery if you work the channel bends where the current keeps things cool and moving. That matches what's happening everywhere south of us: the shallow open flats have gone soft as the water's warmed, but anywhere with structure and current still holding fluke consistently. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through the deeper bends off Mashnee on the last two hours of the ebb, has put keeper fluke in the boat — nothing huge, mostly 16 to 19 inches, but steady.

Here's the one I'm watching hardest right now: Buzzards Bay water has crossed the threshold where bonito and albies start showing, and the west end of the Canal is basically the front door to that water. Wings Neck and Phinneys Harbor sit right in the funnel. I haven't had a confirmed bonito report out of the west end yet, but with the current building the way it is and bait getting concentrated tighter against the seams, I'd bet money we see the first one inside the next week to ten days. If you're itching to be the guy who gets the first report, I'd be working the outgoing tide off Wings Neck with small metal — a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster — worked fast through any nervous water or diving terns.

Slack water's been the tell-all this week. When the current goes flat — and up top it can go dead calm for a solid twenty minutes at both ends — the bite shuts off like someone hit a switch. I've watched guys keep grinding through slack out of stubbornness and it never pays. Better to walk the bank, watch the birds, and be rigged and ready the second that water starts moving again.

Look ahead: with the moon still filling out, expect the current to keep strengthening through the week, which should sharpen those bite windows even more — shorter, harder, more violent. I'd focus effort on the dawn and dusk pushes at the east end for bass and blues, and keep half an eye on the west end for that first bonito sign. If the pattern holds, and there's no reason yet to think it won't, this stays a tide-clock fishery through the first week of August. Know the push, be there when it turns, and don't waste your time in between.
